title: NIC examples and the state

blocks.heading: NIC examples and the state
blocks.text: The syllabus names South Africa, India, the Philippines and Indonesia as illustrative newly industrialising countries; these are syllabus-context examples rather than a current official classification list. State provision of infrastructure, skills or enabling arrangements can support industrial capacity, but the effects depend on relevance, implementation and opportunity cost. A state can help address a missing road connection or skill shortage. It can also spend on facilities that remain unused. To evaluate its role, trace the constraint, the action and the evidence of productive or social benefit. The fictional examples here model that reasoning and are not claims that a named country used a particular policy or achieved a stated result.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Evaluate an illustrative state action
blocks.text: In a fictional NIC-style case, firms have confirmed buyers and trained staff, but a damaged shared road prevents delivery. A state-funded repair with maintenance could address a constraint that individual firms cannot easily solve. If deliveries then become possible, infrastructure has supported capacity use. A second proposal offers unused factory buildings while leaving the road blocked; it is less directly relevant under these facts. This illustrates how to evaluate state action against the productive constraint. It is not an account of events in South Africa, India, the Philippines or Indonesia. Country histories and current rankings are outside this lesson. Topic 2.2 links public plans to implementation and outcomes. A named country or announced expenditure is insufficient evidence of success.

blocks.heading: Apply the connection
blocks.text: Separate a syllabus example, a fictional illustration and evidence of a real policy result. Public spending needs an implementation and outcome connection, as Topic 2.2 explains.
